energy-stores-and-transfers.title: Energy stores and transfers
energy-stores-and-transfers.about: Kinetic and gravitational energy, power, efficiency, specific heat capacity and energy resources.

questions.question: A box of mass $3\ \text{kg}$ is lifted $5\ \text{m}$. How much gravitational potential energy does it gain? ($g = 9.8\ \text{N/kg}$)
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy $= mgh = 3 \times 9.8 \times 5 = 147$ J.

questions.question: A motor transfers 600 J of energy in 20 s. What is its power?
questions.explanation: Power is energy transferred divided by time: 600 divided by 20 = 30 W.

questions.question: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explanation: Wind is renewable because it is replenished as it is used. Coal, gas and nuclear fuel are finite and will eventually run out.

questions.question: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of $2\ \text{kg}$ of water by $10\ ^\circ\text{C}$? (Specific heat capacity of water $= 4200\ \text{J/kg}\,^\circ\text{C}$)
questions.explanation: Energy $= mc\Delta\theta = 2 \times 4200 \times 10 = 84\,000$ J.

electricity.title: Electricity
electricity.about: Current, potential difference and resistance, series and parallel circuits, power and mains electricity.

questions.question: A current of 2 A flows for 30 s. How much charge flows?
questions.explanation: Charge is current multiplied by time: 2 times 30 = 60 C.

questions.question: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery. What is the potential difference across each lamp?
questions.explanation: Components in parallel each have the full potential difference of the supply across them, so each lamp has 6 V. In series they would share it, 3 V each.

questions.question: What happens to the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) as the light intensity increases?
questions.explanation: The resistance of an LDR falls as the light gets brighter. That is why LDRs are used in circuits that switch lights on when it gets dark.

questions.question: A 2 kW heater is switched on for 3 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
questions.explanation: Convert the units first: 2 kW is 2000 W and 3 minutes is 180 s. Energy is power multiplied by time: 2000 times 180 = 360 000 J.

particle-model.title: Particle model
particle-model.about: Density, states of matter, internal energy, latent heat and gas pressure.

questions.question: What is the change of state from solid to liquid called?
questions.explanation: A solid turning into a liquid is melting. Freezing is the reverse, and condensing is a gas turning into a liquid.

questions.question: How much energy is needed to melt $0.5\ \text{kg}$ of ice at $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$? (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $= 334\,000\ \text{J/kg}$)
questions.explanation: Energy $=$ mass $\times$ specific latent heat $= 0.5 \times 334\,000 = 167\,000$ J.

questions.question: A gas is heated in a sealed container of fixed volume. Why does the pressure increase?
options: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
The particles stick to the walls
questions.explanation: Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force, which increases the pressure.

questions.question: A substance is melting at a constant temperature while being heated. What is happening to the energy of its particles?
options: Both their kinetic and potential energy are decreasing
No energy is being transferred to them
Their potential energy is increasing while their kinetic energy stays the same
questions.explanation: The temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change. The energy supplied breaks bonds between particles, increasing their potential energy.

atomic-structure-and-radiation.title: Atomic structure and radiation
atomic-structure-and-radiation.about: The structure of the atom, isotopes, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, and half-life.

questions.question: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Electrons are found in energy levels around the nucleus.

questions.question: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are the most penetrating and need thick lead or concrete to reduce them. Alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few millimetres of aluminium.

questions.question: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to its atomic number?
questions.explanation: In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton and an electron, which is emitted. There is one more proton, so the atomic number goes up by 1. The mass number is unchanged.

questions.question: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 18 hours?
questions.explanation: 18 hours is three half-lives. The amount halves each time: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}$.

forces-and-their-effects.title: Forces and their effects
forces-and-their-effects.about: Scalars and vectors, weight, resultant forces, springs, work done, moments and pressure.

questions.question: Which of these is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: A vector has both size and direction. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Mass, speed and temperature have size only, so they are scalars.

questions.question: A spring has a spring constant of $40\ \text{N/m}$. What force is needed to extend it by $0.15\ \text{m}$?
questions.explanation: Force $=$ spring constant $\times$ extension $= 40 \times 0.15 = 6$ N.

questions.question: A force of 50 N moves a box 4 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
questions.explanation: Work done is force multiplied by distance moved in the direction of the force: 50 times 4 = 200 J.

questions.question: A force of $20\ \text{N}$ acts at a perpendicular distance of $0.3\ \text{m}$ from a pivot. What is the moment of the force?
questions.explanation: Moment $=$ force $\times$ perpendicular distance from the pivot $= 20 \times 0.3 = 6$ N m.

motion-and-newton-s-laws.title: Motion and Newton's laws
motion-and-newton-s-laws.about: Speed, velocity and acceleration, motion graphs, Newton's laws and stopping distances.

questions.question: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the runner's average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time: 100 divided by 20 = 5 m/s.

questions.question: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
options: The object is moving at a steady speed
questions.explanation: A horizontal line means the distance is not changing, so the object is not moving. A steady speed would be a straight sloping line.

questions.question: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph gives the distance travelled. The gradient of the graph gives the acceleration.

questions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates at $2\ \text{m/s}^2$ over a distance of $25\ \text{m}$. What is its final speed? (Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$)
questions.explanation: $v^2 = 0^2 + 2 \times 2 \times 25 = 100$, so $v = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m/s. Remember to take the square root at the end.

momentum.title: Momentum
momentum.about: Momentum, conservation of momentum in collisions, and force as rate of change of momentum.

questions.question: What is the unit of momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, so its unit is kilograms times metres per second: kg m/s.

questions.question: A ball of mass 0.5 kg moves at 12 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity: 0.5 times 12 = 6 kg m/s.

questions.question: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley and they stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?
questions.explanation: Momentum before is 2 times 3 = 6 kg m/s. Momentum is conserved, and the combined mass is 3 kg, so the velocity after is 6 divided by 3 = 2 m/s.

questions.question: The momentum of a car changes by 600 kg m/s in 0.2 s. What is the average force acting on the car?
questions.explanation: Force is change in momentum divided by the time taken: 600 divided by 0.2 = 3000 N. This is why crumple zones, which increase the time, reduce the force.

waves.title: Waves
waves.about: Transverse and longitudinal waves, the wave equation, period, reflection and refraction.

questions.question: What type of wave is a sound wave?
options: A wave that needs no medium
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels. It needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.question: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its period?
questions.explanation: Period is 1 divided by frequency: 1 divided by 50 = 0.02 s. This is the time for one complete wave.

questions.question: Water waves travel at $3\ \text{m/s}$ and have a wavelength of $0.6\ \text{m}$. What is their frequency?
questions.explanation: Rearrange $v = f\lambda$ to get $f = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{3}{0.6} = 5$ Hz.

questions.question: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. What happens to the light?
options: It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends towards the normal
questions.explanation: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. Slowing down makes the ray bend towards the normal. Leaving the glass, it speeds up and bends away again.

electromagnetic-spectrum.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
electromagnetic-spectrum.about: The order, properties, uses and dangers of electromagnetic waves.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used in a television remote control?
questions.explanation: Remote controls send signals using infrared radiation. Infrared is also used in heaters, cooking and thermal imaging cameras.

questions.question: What do all electromagnetic waves have in common?
options: The same speed in a vacuum
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at the same speed in a vacuum. They differ in wavelength and frequency.

questions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave from the Sun causes sunburn and can lead to skin cancer?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation can damage skin cells, causing sunburn, premature ageing and an increased risk of skin cancer.

questions.question: Why are X-rays and gamma rays hazardous to living cells?
options: They heat water in the cells
They are ionising and can damage DNA
questions.explanation: X-rays and gamma rays carry enough energy to ionise atoms. This can damage the DNA in cells, causing mutations that may lead to cancer.

magnetism-and-electromagnetism.title: Magnetism and electromagnetism
magnetism-and-electromagnetism.about: Magnetic fields, electromagnets, the motor effect, generators and transformers.

questions.question: What happens when two north poles are brought close together?
questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Two north poles, or two south poles, push each other apart.

questions.question: Which change makes an electromagnet stronger?
options: Adding more turns to the coil
questions.explanation: An electromagnet is made stronger by more turns on the coil, a larger current or adding an iron core. Reversing the current only swaps the poles.

questions.question: A transformer has 100 turns on its primary coil and 500 turns on its secondary coil. The input potential difference is 12 V. What is the output potential difference?
questions.explanation: The ratio of the potential differences equals the ratio of the turns. The secondary has 5 times as many turns, so the output is 5 times 12 = 60 V.

questions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil of wire and a potential difference is induced. What happens if the magnet is pushed in faster?
options: The induced potential difference is smaller
The induced potential difference is larger
The induced potential difference is unchanged
questions.explanation: Moving the magnet faster makes the magnetic field through the coil change more quickly, which induces a larger potential difference.

space-physics.title: Space physics
space-physics.about: The solar system, orbits, the life cycle of stars, and red-shift.

questions.question: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Gravity provides the force towards the Sun that keeps each planet moving in its orbit.

questions.question: What is the name of the cloud of dust and gas from which a star forms?
questions.explanation: A star forms when gravity pulls together the dust and gas in a nebula. As it collapses it heats up to form a protostar.

questions.question: What process releases energy in a main sequence star such as the Sun?
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explanation: In a main sequence star, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing energy. The outward pressure from fusion balances the inward pull of gravity.

questions.question: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted. What does this show?
options: The galaxies are made of red stars
The galaxies are moving towards us
The galaxies are moving away from us
questions.explanation: Red-shift means the light's wavelength has been stretched, which happens when the source is moving away. More distant galaxies show more red-shift, evidence that the universe is expanding.
